{{Short description|English mathematician, teacher and textbook writer}}

'''James Hann''' (1799–1856) was an English mathematician, teacher and textbook writer.

==Life==
Hann was born at [[Washington, County Durham]], where his father was a colliery smith. After working as a fireman at a pumping-station at [[Hebburn]], he was for several years on one of the steamers used on the [[Tyne River]] for towing vessels. He studied mathematics, in particular the works of [[William Emerson (mathematician)|William Emerson]] the fluxionist.<ref name="DNB">{{cite DNB|wstitle=Hann, James|volume=24}}</ref>

Hann then became a teacher, and kept a school at Friar's Goose, near [[Newcastle upon Tyne|Newcastle]]. An acquaintanceship with [[Wesley S. B. Woolhouse]] the mathematician led to Hann's obtaining a situation as calculator in the [[HM Nautical Almanac Office|Nautical Almanac Office]]. A few years later he was appointed writing-master, and then shortly mathematical master at [[King's College School]], London; this post he held till his death. Among his pupils was [[Henry Fawcett]].<ref name="DNB"/>

Hann was elected a member of the [[Institution of Civil Engineers]] in 1843, and was an honorary member of the [[Philosophical Society of Newcastle-on-Tyne]]. He died in King's College Hospital 17 August 1856, aged 57 years.<ref name="DNB"/>

==Works==
In applied mathematics Hann wrote:<ref name="DNB"/>

* ''Mathematics for Practical Men'', published 1833, with [[Isaac Dodds and Son|Isaac Dodds]] of Gateshead, a friend and owner of one of the steamers on which Hann worked;<ref name="ODNB">{{cite ODNB|id=12206|title=Hann, James|first=Ben|last=Marsden}}</ref>
* ''The Theory of Bridges'', 1843, with [[William Hosking]];<ref name="ODNB"/>
* ''Treatise on the Steam Engine, with Practical Rules'', 1847, for [[John Weale (publisher)|John Weale]];<ref name="ODNB"/>
* ''Principles and Practice of the Machinery of Locomotive Engines'', 1850, for Weale.<ref name="ODNB"/>

In 1841, with [[Olinthus Gregory]], Hann drew up and published ''Tables for the Use of Nautical Men''. He also contributed papers to the ''Diaries'' and other mathematical periodicals.<ref name="DNB"/>

Hann published on mechanics and pure mathematics, works in these areas being for Weale's ''Rudimentary Series'':<ref name="DNB"/><ref name="ODNB"/>

* ''Analytical Geometry'' (later reworked by [[John Radford Young]]);
* ''Treatise on Plane Trigonometry'';
* ''Spherical Trigonometry'';
* ''Examples of the Integral Calculus'';
* ''Examples of the Differential Calculus''.

==Family==
Hann married as a young Man, and had several Children.<ref name="DNB"/>
